summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina removed it from its criminal code in 1996 and Republika Srpska followed in 1998, each through its own entity-level code, so a trans visitor carries no legal exposure on that basis. The age of consent is set at 14 years equally regardless of gender and sexual orientation, with sex below that age treated as statutory rape.

Statutory protection at state level is explicit. The amended Anti-Discrimination Law adopted in 2016 covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics in the terminology used locally; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination had covered sexual orientation and gender expression but omitted gender identity as originally intended. The Sarajevo Open Centre presented the 2016 amendments together with the Agency for Gender Equality after public consultations in autumn 2015.

Bias-motivated violence is treated as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing. In April 2016 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina amended its Criminal Code to criminalise hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, the text published on 15 June 2016, and comparable bans operate in Republika Srpska and Brčko District.

The principal risk a trans visitor faces is violence rather than prosecution. The Queer Sarajevo Festival in 2008 was stormed by football fans and religious extremists shouting death threats; eight people including a policeman were injured, and in 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled that authorities had failed to protect participants' freedom of assembly. Organised anti-LGBT violence has occurred even where police coordination was in place: the Sarajevo Open Centre said it had arranged security with police about three weeks before the attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers reported by Human Rights Watch on 4 February 2014, and HRW's Lydia Gall demanded prosecution of the attackers.

Public visibility has expanded alongside that risk. The first Pride march in Bosnia and Herzegovina was held in Sarajevo on 9 September 2019 with an estimated 2,000 marchers. In March 2023 police in Banja Luka cancelled LGBTQ film screenings over security concerns and activists were chased and attacked afterwards. The Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024, published 13 June 2024, records a number of negative events over the past year with significant impact and describes a long-visible worsening trend as becoming increasingly evident.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples at national or subnational level. The Constitution is silent on gender eligibility for marriage, both entities' family codes limit marriage to opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couple households are not eligible for the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples. On 19 October 2018 the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a request to legalise civil unions; a working group established in January 2020 had its start postponed because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion measured in the sources is hostile to relationship recognition. A 2015 survey found 19% of the population supported granting same-sex couples some marriage-associated rights, and a 2017 Pew poll found 13% support for same-sex marriage against 84% opposed. The same 2015 survey found 48% of Bosnians would try to 'cure' their child if the child came out as gay and 16% would stop communicating with that child.

The protection regime is split across the two entities, so the wording and reach of hate-crime provisions differ by where an incident occurs: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's 2016 amendment is documented in detail, while Republika Srpska runs its own separate regime and Brčko District its own as well.

Visibility gains appear geographically contained. A 2021 study found the 2019 Sarajevo Pride parade increased support for LGBT activism only in Sarajevo, not nationwide, which bears on expectations outside the capital.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice. The Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions changes to identity documents on 'completed' medical transition, and the constraints are described as discriminatory and degrading; legal gender change is available only after sex reassignment surgery and other medical treatments.

Healthcare is a documented site of discrimination for residents. A 2017 PLOS ONE qualitative study documents the stigma and discrimination men who have sex with men experience from healthcare professionals and the general community.

The civil-union route remains unfinished for residents: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's October 2018 request to legalise civil unions produced a working group in January 2020 whose start was postponed because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory states that Republika Srpska and Brčko District have hate-crime bans comparable to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's, but does not supply their statutory wording, so whether each names gender identity with the same specificity is not sourced here.

Not sourced: no inventory item addresses border or airport screening, presentation of identity documents at entry, or access to gendered facilities, so any trans-specific dimension of those procedures is unestablished rather than absent.

Unresolved: enforcement of the 2016 Anti-Discrimination Law is not evidenced by case outcomes in the inventory, and whether the January 2020 civil-union working group has since convened is not stated beyond the recorded postponement.
